OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I have to refer, with profound sorrow, to 
the passing away of Shri Ebrahim Sulaiman Sait, a former Member of this 
House on the 27th April, 2005 at the age of 83 years. 
Born at Bangalore in November, 1922, Shri Sulaiman Sait had his education 
at St. Josseph College, Bangalore. 
A businessman and teacher by profession, Shri Sulaiman Sait was actively 
associated with various social, political and cultural organisations and took keen 
interest in Islamic History and Theology, Urdu poetry and minority problems. 
Shri Sulaiman Sait was Secretary of the Kerala State Muslim League in 1961 
and its Vice-President from 1962 to 1973 and elected the President of the Indian 
Union Muslim League in 1973. He was also General Secretary of the All India 
Muslim Personal Law Board and All India President of the Indian National 
League. 
Shri Sulaiman Sait represented the State of Kerala in this House from April, 
1960 to April, 1966. He was also a Member of the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, 
Seventh, Eighth, Ninth and Tenth Lok Sabha. 
Shri Sulaiman Sait had a few publications jn Urdu to his credit. He was also an 
editor of a magazine published by the Urdu Society of the Aligarh Muslim 
University. 
A widely travelled person, Shri Sulaiman Sait visited many countries as part of 
Indian Delegations and represented the country in many international events. He 
was a member of the Indian Parliamentary Delegation to Afghanisatian, Iran and 
Turkey in 1971 and to Switzerland and London in 1975. 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2005] 
In the passing away of Shri Ebrahim Sulaiman Sait, the country has lost a 
veteran Parliamentarian, a renowned social worker and a champion of minority 
rights. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Ebrahim Sulaiman Sait. 
I request hon. Members to rise in th eir seats and observe silence for one 
minute as a mark of respect to the departed soul. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-Generalirill convey to the members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

(a) whether on the eve of the recent visit of Pakistan's President to New Delhi, Pak

(b) if so, what was Government's reaction and response thereto; 
(c) whether it is a fact that while India wants authentication of the maps or the actual 
ground position line before any pull back, Pakistan wants the pre-1972 troops positions 
to be recognized; 
(d) whether the matter was discussed during the recent Pak President's visit to New 
Delhi; and 
(e) if so, the outcome thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH): (a) to (e) A

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2005] 
Statement 
(a) There have been reports of Pakistan Foreign Minister indicating Pakistan's 
willingness to withdraw its forces from Siachen area but linking it to certain 
unacceptable conditions. 
(b) Does not apply. 
(c) Our position on the issue is that the authentication of the present position has to 
be the first step, before any redeployment is considered. 
(d) and (e) During Pakistan President Pervez Musharraf's visit to New Delhi from 
April 16-18-2005, it was agreed that the existing institutional mechanisms should 
convene discussions immediately with a view to finding mutually acceptable solution on 
the issue expeditiously. 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Sir, during his recent visit, the Pakistan President 
had spoken about softening of hearts and opening of borders. Of course, we all want 
more people-to-people contact, more cultural and political exchanges, and closer trade 
and economic ties, yet we cannot afford to take any risks on national security. 
In this context, I would like to know whether Siachin is of great strategic 
importance and withdrawal of troops from Siachin opens India to grave security risks. 
What specific steps are being taken to safeguard our national interests? 
SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: Sir, during the visit of the President of Pakistan 
recently, this matter did come up; but it came up in greater detail when I went to Pakistan 
and held talks with my counterpart, the Foreign Minister, Mr. Khurshid Kasuri, and 
during the meeting of our Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singh and President 
Musharraf only a few days ago, the two Heads directed us that the Defence Secretaries 
of both the countries should meet within the month of May, latest by June, to tackle this 
problem to find a mutually-acceptable solution to both the issues with regard to Siachin. I 
only want to say that the Siachin ceasefire has now held for almost three years, and 
there is no real tension. We are all concerned with all the national intersts in this regard, 
and India's vital national interests will not be jeopardised in any way. 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Sir, de spite all the friendly talks and 
exchange of pleasantries with the Pakistan President, terrorists concentrations and 
camps remain intact along the borders and the LOC. May I

Indo-China Boundary Dispute 
*481. SHRI RAJ NATH SI NGH: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) how far the talks between India and China have progressed to settle the boundary 
dispute between the two countries; 
(b) the details of such talks; 
(c) whether Government plan to take all the political parties into confidence before 
reaching a final agreement with China; and 
(d) If not, the reasons behind it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) There have been five meetings so far between the Special Representatives of 
India and China on the boundary question. These talks 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2005] 
resulted in the signing of the "Agreement on the Political Parameters and Guiding Principles 
for the Settlement of the India-China Boundary Question" between the two sides on April 
11,2005 during the recent visit of the Chinese Premier to India. Based on the parameters 
and principles laid down in the Agreement, the Special Representatives have been tasked to 
continue their consultations with the objective of arriving at an agreed framework for a 
boundary settlement, which will provide the basis for the delineation and demarcation of 
the India-China boundary to be subsequently undertaken by civil and military officials 
and surveyors of the two sides. In addition, the India-China Joint Working Group on the 
boundary question, which is engaged in tasks relating to clarification and confirmation of 
the line of actual control and establishment of confidence building measures in the India-
China border areas, continues its discussions. 
(c) and (d) Government's policy towards China is characterized by continuity and 
consensus. In dealing with complex issues like the boundary question, it has been 
Government's endeavour to consult political parties and seek understanding and support of 
the Parliament.

Shoot up in unemployment rate 
*491. SHRI EKANATH K.THAKUR: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the unemployment rate for the country has shot 
up significantly from 8.87 percent in 2001-02 to 9.11 percent in 2004-05; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that employment in the organized sector has 
declined between 2001 and 2003 in both public and private sectors; and 
(c) if so, the action proposed in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRASEKHAR RAO) (a) to (c): Estimates of employment and 
unemployment are obtained through quinquennial labour surveys carried out 
by National Sample Survey Organisation. Last such survey was undertaken 
during 1999-2000. As per these surveys, unemployment rate in the country on 
current daily status basis has gone up from approximately 6.03 percent in 
1993-94 to 7.32 percent in 1999-2000 
It is a fact that employment in both  Public and Private organised sectors 
has gone down during the period 2001-2003. 
Government is tackling the problem of unemployment in its various facets. 
In view of the fact that scope for additional employment creation is not much 
in the organised sector, government is targeting creation of around 5 crore 
employment opportunities during the 10th Plan period both in organised and 
unorganised sectors taken together with special emphasis on labour intensive 
sectors such as agriculture, irrigatio n, agro-forestry, small and medium 
enterprises, information communication technology, tourism and other 
services. Besides this, a National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill has been 
introduced in Parliament, which provides for 100 days of employment in a 
year for poor families in the rural areas. A food for work programme has 
already been launched in selected backward districts of the country.

†3724. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased

supplied to steel companies; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. DASARI 
NARAYANA RAO): (a) Coal Companies supply non-coking/non linked 
washed coking coal to the power plants  (except most of the pit-head power 
plants of NTPC) at the price notified by CIL. Washery Middlings/ Washed Coal 
(Power/Washed Non-coking coal is supplied to some of the Power Plants at the 
prices notifed by the Coal companies. The basis for fixation of price through

(iii) Demand and supply scenario,and

long term Fuel Supply Agreement (FSA). The FSA contains a price escalation formula and 
prices of coal supplied to these pit-head power plants are arrived at each year on the 
basis of the said formula taking the base price as applicable on the date of implementation 
of FSA. 
(b) Yes, Sir. the difference in price of coking, coal and the coal being supplied to the 
steel companies is arising out of the difference between the prices of two products. The 
price of raw coking coal is notified by CIL whereas the price of washed coking coal, which 
is a value added product, is negotiated with Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL) every year 
bilaterally. Other steel companies like IISCO, TISCO and RINL either offer a price 
higher than the negotiated price or adopt the same price as negotiated with SAIL. 
(c) the basic price of coking coal ranges between Rs. 930/- per tonne to Rs. 2960/- per

3741. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) to(e) 
The Universal Postal Union (UPU), a specialized agency of the United Nations 
with a membership of 190 countries decided to set up a fund called the Quality of 
Service Fund at the 22nd UPU Congress held in 1999 at Beijing. The objective of the Fund 
was to bring about improvement in the quality of letter mail processing and delivery 
in developing postal 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2005] 
administrations. It was decided that this Fund would be maintained through a 7.5% 
increase accepted by Industr ialised Countries (ICs) on the payments made to 
postal administrations of Developing Countries (DCs) for handling and delivery 
charges of total-mail sent by ICs to DCs. The fund is administered by a nine 
member Board of Trustees (BOT), of the member administrations of the Universal 
Postal Union. The BOT approves funds to be given to creditor administrations 
(DCs) of the QSF on the basis of project proposal submitted by the 
administrations for improvement in the quality of service. These projects needs to 
be linked to one of the following six areas:— 
access to services, 
speed and reliability, 
security, 
liability and handling of inquiries, 
customer satisfaction or design 
implementation of cost accounting system. 
India, being one of the developing countries, is a beneficiary of the QSF. 
One project has been implemented so fa r. Under this project, the 4 Airmail 
Offices of Exchange at Delhi (Delhi),  Kolkata (West Bengal), Chennai (Tamil 
Nadu) and Mumbai (Maharashtra) have been computerized.

 3759.  SHRI LALIT SURI: 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY:

a result thereof, agreement wise; and 
(e) in what manner the implementation thereof would be watched and ensured? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(RAO INDERJEET SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. Honourable Prime Minister visited 
Mauritius from 30 March to 2 April 2005. 
(b) A broad range of issues of mutual interest were discussed during this visit. 
India has extremely close relations with Mauritius and a number of proposals for 
boosting cooperation between the two countries in the fields of commerce, economy, 
defence, small scale industries, oil were discussed. It is envisaged that as a result of 
this visit Indo-Mauritian ties will be further strengthened and consolidated. 
111 

RAJYASABHA [28 April, 2005] 
(c) Four agreements were signed during this visit which are as 
follows: 
(i) Agreement for setting up of a Joint Working Group on combating 
international Terrorism, 
(ii) MoU relating to Bilateral Air Services between India and Mauritius (iii) 
MoU on Cooperation in the field of Protection of the Environment. 
(iv) MoU on offering a fresh line of Credit of US$10 million for the Baie du 
Tombeau Sewerage Project. 
(d) Salient features of above agreements: 
I. Agreement for setting up of a Joint Working Group on combating 
international Terrorism: The main objectives of setting up a Joint Working 
Group on Terrorism are as follows: 
(i) Share experience in combating inte rnational terrorism, organized crime 
and illicit trafficking in arms, narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances and 
their linkages; 
(ii) Coordinate approaches to combat such international terrorism and 
terrorist acts, organized crime, syndicates and groups dealing in drug 
trafficking, trafficking in arms, money laundering and other economic 
offences; 
(iii) Exchange information on the activities of terrorist and organized 
criminal groups and thei r associates that may operate from or use the 
territories of either party; 
(iv) Establish an institutional framework for such cooperation. 
II. MoU relating to Bilateral Air Services between India and 
Mauritius: 
(i) This aims to expand, increase and improve the frequency of air services 
between India and Mauritius. 
(ii) It gives fifth freedom traffic rights to designated airline from India in 
Mauritius for onward fights to two points in South Africa. Similarly, it grants to 
designated airlines from Mauritius in India for onward flights to Pakistan and 
China. 
III. MOU on Cooperation in the field of Protection of the 
Environment: 
This aims to foster and establish close cooperation between India and 
Mauritius for protection and improvement of their environment. It envisages 
adoption of a number of measures with following objectives in view: 
112 

[28 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) prevention of Coastal Erosion, Lagoon Pollution, loss of biodiversity and 
damage of the reef system; (b) to deal effectively with various problems relating to 
pollution; (c) to exchange relevant information in this regard; (d) to take 
effective steps to ensure treatment of waste water from industries and sugar mills; 
(e) to evolve low cost and environmentally sound technologies for pollution 
control; (f) to take various other measures as appropriate to bring about 
improvement of environment and its protection. 
IV. MOU on offering a fresh line of  Credit of US$10 million for the 
Baie du Tombeau Sewerage Project: 
This credit line will be operated by Exim Bank of India as per the norms and 
procedures in force and will be utilized by Government of Mauritius for 
implementing Baie du Tombeau Sewerage Project. 
As regards the benefits which will accrue to India from these Agreements/ MOUs: 
It is hoped that these Agreements/M oUs will lead to increased economic 
cooperation between India and Mauritiu s and to improved communications 
between them. It is also envisaged that they will help both the countries to 
take requisite measures for better ensuring their internal security as well as for 
better protection and improvement of their environment. 
(e) The bilateral relations between India and Mauritius are reviewed on a regular 
basis. There is continuous consultation and interaction between India and 
Mauritius at different levels. It would thus be ensured that these agreements are 
being implemented.

(SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. India has ratified the 1994 
Convention on Nuclear Safety. The Instrument of Ratification was submitted on 
March 31,2005 to the Director General, International Atomic Energy Agency, 
who is the Depository of the Convention. India shares the objective of the 
Convention of maintaining a high level of nuclear safety worldwide through the 
enhancement of national measures and international cooperation, including in safety-
related technical cooperation. This incentive Convention has been ratified by all 
countries producing nuclear power.

such actions, or such incidents being misinterpreted by the other." During the 
visit of External Affairs Minister Shri Natwar Singh to Pakistan in February

3772. SHRI E.M. SUDARSANA NATC HIAPPAN: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (c) Pakistan 
Singificant development have taken place in India-Pakistan relations since 
April 2003. Relations have been resotred at the level of High Commissioners; 
transport and communication links have resumed; one round of Composite 
Dialogue has been completed; a series of technical level and Composite Dialogue 
related meetings have been held on schedule. Another round has been initiated with 
the Foreign Secretary level talks in December 2004. 
122 

[28 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
 
 People to people exchange are taking place across the supectrum in large 
numbers. There has been a resumption of visits by pilgrim groups. Our High 
Commission is issuing close to 10,000 visas per month. 
The bilateral process has been given impetus through maintenance of high 
level contacts. The meeting between Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh and 
President Musharraf in New York in September 2004 was followed by the visit of 
Prime Minister Shaukat Aziz to New Delhi on November 23-24,2004. February 
2005 saw a bilateral visit by an Indian EAM to Pakistan after a gap of almost 16 
years. President Musharraf visited India from April 16-18, 2005; the visit took 
bilateral relations forward in a significant way. 
The Srinagar Muzaffrabad bus has already been operationalized from April 
7,2005; agreements have been reached to start bus services between Lahore and 
Amritsar, including to religious places such as Nankana Sahib. Pakistan also 
agreed for restoration of the Khokrapar-Munnabao rail till January 1, 2006 . 
The ceasefire being observed along the International Border, the LOC, and the 
AGPL in Siachen, with the exception of two incidents, has held for more than a 
year. 
India has agreed to discuss the proposal of a pipeline through Pakistan, subject 
to satisfaction of our concerns on secu rity and adequate supplies. Agreements 
would be concluded in the coming months on Pre-notification of Missile Tests , 
and between Coast Guards and Pakistan's  Maritime Security Agency, as well 
as between the narcotics control authorities of the two countries. Discussions 
would begin on Agreements on Preventing Incidents at Sea, and Reducing the 
Risk of Nuclear Accident or Unauthroised use of Nuclear Weapons. 
Progress has been made in meetings on conventional and nuclear CBMs, 
and a Joint Survey of the boundary pillars in the International B oundary in the 
Sir Creek has also been successfully concluded in January 2005. 
Significant progress has been achieved on the humanitarian issue of 
fishermen and civilian detainess. During the Foreign Secretary level talks in 
December 2004, it was inter alia agreed that: 
• Immediate notification would be provided to the respective High 
Commissions through the Foreign Ministries of arrested 
Pakistani/Indian nationals; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2005] 
• Consular access would be provided within three months of 
apprehension; 
• Repatriation would be done immediately after completion of 
sentence and nationality verification; 
• A mechanism would be introduced for early repartiation, without 
sentencing of inadvertent crossers; 
• A similar mechanissm would be established for early release, without 
sentencing of those under 16 apprehended by either side. 
Since then, Pakistan, has released 266 Indian fishermen in January 2005 it 
has released additional 528 Indian fishermen and 36 civilian prisoners in 
March 2005. India has provided consular access to 113 civilian prisoners in 2005 
and 22 civilian prisoners are currently being released in April 2005. We have 
released 156 out of 194 Pakistani fishermen in our custody on April 19, 2005. 
Thus meaningful progress has been achieved in the process of 
normalization of India-Pakistan relations. Government are committed to 
continuing the present process of building confidence, enhancing cooperation 
and dialogue in an atmoshpere free from terrorism and violence, and to discuss any 
outstanding bilateral issue with Pakistan, including Jammu and Kashmir. 
Nepal 
India attaches high priority to its relations with Nepal. As a neighbour and 
close friend we continue to support all efforts in Nepal in restoration of peace and 
stability in the country. India has consistently held the view that the problems 
confronting Nepal including the Maoist insurgency can be addressed effectively 
only or the basis of a national consensus between the two constitutional forces, 
namely multi-party democracy and constitutional monarcy. 
Considerable progress has been made in our cooperation with Nepal in the area 
of border security and management. New mechnisms have been established to 
strengthen cross-border coordination and exchange of information. Tests of a 
new Extradition Treaty and an Agreemen t on Mutual Legal Assistance in 
Criminal Matters have been finalized. Several infrastructure projects for 
development of border infrastructure have been launched. These projects would 
facilitate bilateral ec onomic cooperation and also contribute towards 
strengthening security in border areas.

House not to proceed with the sale of F-16 to Pakistan; and

(SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) In the first session of 109th U.S. Congress, Gary

Americans, introduced a bill "to prohibit the provision of United States military 
assistance and the sale, transfer, or licensing of United State military 
equipment or technology to Pakistan". The bill makes such military assistance to

and Indian-Americans in the House of Representatives. The letter opposed F-16 
sale to Pakistan and asked the members of the House to join in sending a letter to 
President Bush to this effect It referred to the President Bush's National Security 
Strategy released in 2002, which recognized the importance of changing the 
dynamic between the United States and India. It underscored that if the United 
States provided F-16s to Pakistan, plan es inherently capable of delivering 
nuclear weapons, the message would be that U.S.'s true strategic partner in 
South Asia was Pakistan and such a message would squander an opportunity to 
continue building the strong relationship that the United States needed with India.

Bringing down of Poverty Ratio 
†3810. SHRI MANGANILAL MANDAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several effective programmes are being                               
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

[28 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
implemented in the country to bring down the poverty ratio during the Tenth Five 
Year Plan by the year 2007; and 
(b) if so, target set to bring down the poverty ratio during the Tenth Plan and the 
details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN) (a) Yes, Sir. It is a fact that serveral effective programmes 
are being implemented in the country to bring down the poverty ratio during the Tenth 
Five Year Plan by the year 2007. 
The programmes which are being implemented in the rural areas by Ministry of 
Rural Development for upliftment of BPL families are (i) Sampoorna Grameen 
Rozgar Yojana (SGRY), (ii) Swaranjayati Gram Swarozar Yojana (SGSY), (iii) 
Indira Awas Yojana (IAY) and (iv) National Food for Works Programme 
(NFFWP). 
The programme which is being implemented in the urban areas for poverty 
alleviation is Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana (SJSRY). The programme targets the 
urban poor, defined as those living Below the Poverty Line, as defined from time to time. 
The Programme is applicable to all urban towns in India. The Programme is 
implemented on a whole town basis with special emphasis on urban poor clusters. In 
addition to this, the Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY), and National 
Slum Development Programmes (NSDP) which are meant for providing shelter/ 
upgradation of shelter and environmental upgradation for the urban slum dwellers, also 
contribute indirectly toward poverty alleviation. 
In addition, under the new scheme of the Targeted Public Distribution System 
(TPDS) each poor family is entitled to 35 kgs of foodgrains. In order to make the 
TPDS more focused and targeted towards the very poor category, the "Antyodaya Anna 
Yojana" provides 35 kgs of foodgrains to the poorest of the poor families at a highly 
subsidized rate of Rs 2 per kg., for wheat and Rs. 3 per kg., for rice. In the recent 
budget presented on 28-02-05 it was announced that the coverage of Antyodaya Anna 
Yojana will be increased from 2.0 crore (BPL) families to 2.5 crore families in 
2005. 
(b) The Tenth Five Year Plan period (2002-07) for the first time has set a target for 
reduction of poverty by 5 percentage points by 2007 and by 15, percentage points by 
2012.

Earthquake Resistant Techniques in Delhi 
†3822. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECH-
NOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) to what extent Delhi is safe so far as the earthquake is concerned; 
(b) whether Government would provide low cost earthquake resistant 
technique for the buildings to be constructed in Delhi; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL) (a) As per the seismic zoning map of 
India published by Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) the country has been 
divided into four seismic zones, namely Zone II, III, IV and V. While Zone V is 
considered to be most seismically active, Zone II is the least. As per this map 
Delhi falls in Zone IV. 
(b) and (c) The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) has published various 
guidelines and codes for design and c onstruction of earthquake resistant 
structures, as well as retrofitting of buildings etc. Losses due to earthquakes can 
considerably be reduced if these guid elines/codes are fo llowed during new 
constructions/strengthening of existing structures etc.

Launching of ASTROSAT Project 
3852. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have approved ASTROSAT Project last 
year; 
(b) if so, the aims and objectives of this project; and 
(c) by when ASTROSAT is going to be launched? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE (SHRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The main goal of ASTROSAT mission is to launch a space based multiwavelength 
astronomical observatory for studies in the frontier areas of high energy astronomy and 
astrophysics. The scientifc objectives include the following: 
* Multiwavelength studies of galactic and extra galactic stellar objects by near 
simultaneous measurement of X-ray, ultraviolet and optical emissions from the 
sources. 
* To study stellar phenomena using the observations covering the wavelength band 
in visible, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma-rays regions. 
* Detailed study of the spectra of neutron star and black hole binaries, AGNs (Active 
Galactic Nuclei), SNRs (Supernova Remnants) etc. 
* High sensitivity timing observations of periodic and aperiodic variations. 
* Detection and study of pulsars.

Demand for Granting Classical Language Status to Kannada 
SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY (Karnataka): Sir, it was a long-overdue step by the 
Government of India to have accorded the 'Classical Language' status to Tamil, with 
its lexical richness and antiquity, spanning several centuries. 
Going by the criteria set for recognition of a language as a Classical one, Kannada 
rightfully qualifies for accord of a similar status. On all accounts—antiquity, ancient body of 
literature, original living traditions and continuity—Kannada has impeccable credentials, as 
documented by the UNESCO in its monograph "ASIA SCRIPTS' which ranks 'Kannada' 
among the major scripts of the world. 
Sir, beyond its lexical purity, Kannada transcends the creative aspects further on to 
canonized local knowledge systems, grammatical traditions, dictionaries, encyclopaedias, 
books on science, medicine agriculture etc. 
Sir, a well-documented case has already been made by the Government of 
Karnataka, in its communication to the hon. Prime Minister of India, which I commend, 
be subjected to a critical evaluation by the Sahitya Academy which has access to a vast 
repository of books and reference works. Compared to Hebrew and Chinese writing 
systems that claim an antiquity of three millennia, among Indian languages only Tamil' 
and 'Kannada' have a long and enduring history of writing. I request the Government of India 
to accord a 'Classical Language' status to Kannada.

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2005] 
First of all, before I start responding to the issues raised by the hon. Members, I 
would like to place on record the services which the Indian Armed Forces rendered 
over the years and, particularly, on two recent occasions. When the Tsunami struck in the 
early hours of 26th December, 2004, the response of the Indian Armed Forces were 
unique. All the three wings of the Armed Forces, the Air Force, the Navy and the Army, 
came forward and they not only provided relief and succour to our people, whether it was 
Andaman and Car Nicobar Islands or the coastal districts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra 
Pradesh and Pondicherry, but also extended their support to the neighbouring countries, 
Maldives, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. My colleague, the hon. Minister of External Affairs, is 
also present here. He has received appreciation from almost all these countries for the 
unique contribution made by the Indian Armed Forces. Sir, not only on the sea, but also 
on the land a peculiar situation arose some time in February. There was a huge 
snowfall, a huge avalanche, on the mountains and thousands of people were to be rescued 
by the Indian Air Force and they did so. Even in this hour of distress and difficulty, while the 
rescue operations were going on, a young mother gave birth to a child and the Armed 
Forces took care of them and the new-born child and the mother were treated well and they 
were safe. These persons, whether it is in the desert of Rajasthan or on the snow-capped 
mountains or in the dense forests of the North-East, pass sleepless nights to protect our 
borders and to ensure that we in the main land live in peace. Therefore, I do feel that we 
should appreciate their contributions and recognise the services rendered by them. 
The Indian Army has very long history. I am not going back to the date of history. Many 
of my colleagues are fully aware of it. It was raised as a colonial force in 1776. After the 
battle of Plazy, the then East Indian Company raised this force. Thereafter, it was 
converted into three Presidency Provincial Forces, the Madras Presidency, the Bengal 
Presidency and the Bombay Presidency. At that time, there was no Mumbai; it was 
Bombay. Later, they were converted into the Indian Army. Since the raising of these 
forces, for more than 200 years, these forces have established their credibility and they 
have shown their commitment, especially, to the democratic institutions to the core of their 
heart. 
As a student of History, sometimes, I wonder what was inherent in the system when we 
found I would not mention the name of the countries with whom we got Independence, almost, 
at the same time, in the first part of the last Century—that one after another, in those 
countries, democratic

make a few remarks. 
First of all, I must concentrate on the alternative energy sources, particularly because 
this is an area amenable to good technology, good innovations, and this aspect has been 
very well brought out in recent times, thanks to the Ministry and all those who have been 
working with the Ministry in this particular area. So, first of all, I should like to comment on 
the type of steps that they have taken-to promote this very difficult but vital area; and it is 
not just complementing the efforts of the main power systems, but much more than that, it 
is providing a cleaner environment in terms of energy production. 
The first part I would like to say, Mr. Vice-Chairman, is that we have something like 
80,000 MW of additional power generation during 1998-2008. If we just take two or three 
areas like bio-gas, or, small hydro projects and so on, and if you put a target of something 
like 20-30,000 MW that has to be produced in the next four to five years, what does it mean

Ministry of Non-conventional Energy Sources for working out a plan of action? I think, in 
view of the success that they have achieved so far, in view of the ideas that they have

level of something like 20-30,000 MW from the current 5,500 MW, which is the 
present level of production for the alternative energy. It will be a very worthwhile exercise 
to do and to support that kind of effort from the point of producing more of this kind of

The second part that I would like to mention is regarding photovoltaic system. 
Certainly, it is always said to be an expensive business primarily because of the fact that 
one approaches it through the silicon technology. More recently, there have been very 
interesting developments, Mr. Vice-Chairman, which are related to coming out with a 
polymer-based system which can dispense with the silicon technology and the present 
assessment is to cut down the cost by about almost one-fourth to the persent level in 
the solar photovoltaic system. This is something which can be a very interesting route 
for the country to take in case we need to pursue that and if one looks at the potential 
and the real level of achievement, we see that it is not more than four per cent of the 
production of solar photovoltaic power in terms of the potential. Also, it is interesting to note 
that we have been able to export this particular component abroad. In fact, the current 
level of production has dipped this year, primarily because there has been a substantial 
export of this component of the source of power. This is a very interesting aspect of the 
development that has happened. The third aspect that I would like to talk about, Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, is related to hydrogen. Nobody has mentioned about hydrogen, it is 
the source for the energy of the future. I am happy that this country is working currently in 
the hydrogen related technologies, whether it is related to production, storage, 
transportation and applications. 
But, it is sub-critical. But, what is important is, right now, it cannot be better than that 
simply because we just don't have the resources, both the manpower as well as the 
infrastructure, to absorb higher level of fundings in the area of hydrogen. But, what is also 
redeeming to note is the fact that we have a level of development currently in this area 
which is comparable to what we have elsewhere too. This is another aspect of this Hydro-
gen Technology. This is one area which is amenable for international co-operation, 
currently. 
So, because of the fact that we have a level of work that is going on at

further work in this country. I am sure that we could be a leader in the area of

going on in the area of transportation, development of fuel cells and so on. But, 
that is an area of the future and we shoul d support them to the extent that they

opment and production. So, Sir, these were  the three important points which I 
wanted to make. Thank you very much.
